text.title: Spring @Async Worked Examples
text.summary: End-to-end conversion of a synchronous email send into a Spring @Async fan-out, plus the CompletableFuture.allOf composition pattern the rules make possible.

example.note: Context: brownfield Boot 3.4 monolith. `OrderController.placeOrder()` inline-calls `emailService.send()`; p99 latency is 800 ms and the email vendor contributes roughly 400 ms of it.

Step 1 — confirm the send is fire-and-forget (no caller waits on the result) and carries no `@Transactional`, so it is eligible. Check the bean split: `OrderController` calls `NotificationService`, already a separate bean, so `no-self-invocation` is satisfied without extraction.

Step 2 — create `AsyncConfig` with an `emailExecutor` (core 4, max 8, queue 100, `CallerRunsPolicy`, `setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true)` with a 60 s drain, and a `TaskDecorator` copying MDC + `SecurityContext`), per `named-executor`, `caller-runs-backpressure`, `graceful-shutdown` and `taskdecorator-context`.
Step 3 — annotate `NotificationService.sendOrderConfirmation` with `@Async("emailExecutor")` and change the return type to `CompletableFuture<Void>` per `completablefuture-return`.
Step 4 — register the `executor.*` Micrometer gauges and an `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler` that logs and increments a `notification.error` counter.
Step 5 — test with `Awaitility.await().atMost(2, SECONDS).untilAsserted(...)` against a WireMock SMTP stub, then run `scripts/spring-async-audit.sh` and require 0 violations.
Result: p99 drops from 800 ms to 380 ms, the `notification.error` metric becomes visible in Grafana, and a deploy drains the queue instead of dropping mail.

Returning `CompletableFuture` rather than `void` is what makes `allOf` and `exceptionally` available; a `void` `@Async` method would have swallowed both failures silently. `runAsync` without an executor argument uses the common ForkJoinPool — pass the named executor explicitly when the inner work is itself blocking.
